slot.brief: Ask why aryl/vinyl halides fail in Williamson synthesis, or which of the given haloalkane + alkoxide pairs gives ether cleanly vs elimination; test the conceptual condition.

stem: The ether-forming step in Williamson synthesis is usually an $S_\mathrm{N}2$ reaction. Why are aryl and vinyl halides unsuitable substrates for this step?
options: The carbon bonded to X is $sp^2$-hybridised; the C–X bond has partial double-bond character, hindering backside attack.
Ionisation of the C–X bond readily forms a resonance-stabilised aryl or vinyl carbocation, favouring $S_\mathrm{N}1$.
They lack a β-hydrogen, so the alkoxide cannot begin the substitution by removing a proton.
Alkoxide ions are too weak as nucleophiles to displace halide ions from carbon.

verdicts.working: Williamson ether synthesis requires backside SN2 attack. Aryl and vinyl C–X bonds are at sp² carbons and have partial double-bond character, preventing effective backside attack.

working:
Williamson ether formation: $\text{RO}^- + \text{R'X} \xrightarrow{S_\mathrm{N}2} \text{ROR'} + \text{X}^-$.
Aryl and vinyl halides have $sp^2$ C–X bonds with partial double-bond character; backside attack is unfavourable. Independent check: Williamson ether synthesis requires backside SN2 attack. Aryl and vinyl C–X bonds are at sp² carbons and have partial double-bond character, preventing effective backside attack.
solution: Williamson ether synthesis proceeds by backside $S_\mathrm{N}2$ attack. In aryl and vinyl halides, the C–X bond is attached to an $sp^2$-hybridised carbon and has partial double-bond character, hindering this attack.
